items.answer: Profile the task complexity, benchmark on a 100–200 sample golden dataset (not leaderboards), do cost-breakeven math, and accept the smaller model when Δaccuracy is within SLO — fine-tuning with QLoRA for $20–100 typically closes the remaining gap.

items.title: Trim prompts + cache embeddings — before/after cost breakdown?
items.prompt: Trim prompts + cache embeddings — before/after cost breakdown?
items.answer: Prompt trimming saves 75-80% of generation cost via reranking to top-3 chunks (5× context reduction), manual audit, LLMLingua, and output caps; embedding caching saves 95% of document embedding API calls via SHA-256 hash-match at ingestion, delivering latency and rate-limit benefits more than dollar savings — validate each step on a 200-query golden dataset.

items.title: Multi-layer caching: retrieval, prompt, response?
items.prompt: Multi-layer caching: retrieval, prompt, response?
items.answer: Multi-layer caching stacks three independent wins: L3 semantic response cache (30% hit, GPTCache/Redis-FAISS, cosine > 0.93), L2 LLM prefix cache (50–90% discount on static system-prompt tokens), and L1 retrieval cache (embedding SHA-256 hash + ANN result Redis TTL) — together cutting 60–70% of GenAI pipeline cost with namespace-scoped invalidation on content updates.

items.title: Model tiering — small distilled vs large LLM?
items.prompt: Model tiering — small distilled vs large LLM?
items.answer: Route 60–80% of low-complexity queries to a cheap fast model (a small fast model, $1/M) via a lightweight complexity classifier, reserve the frontier model for the hard 5–10%, validate routing accuracy on a golden set, and monitor per-tier quality drift — typically yields 70–80% cost reduction on routed traffic.

items.title: Prompt compression?
items.prompt: Prompt compression?
items.answer: Compress prompts in four ordered layers — rerank to top-3 chunks (85% context reduction, lossless), summarize conversation history, manually audit the system prompt, then optionally apply LLMLingua (2–5× lossy compression) — and separately cap output tokens via max_tokens + structured JSON, since output costs 5× more than input per token.

items.title: Budget estimate for RAG at enterprise scale (e.g. 300K legal contracts)?
items.prompt: Budget estimate for RAG at enterprise scale (e.g. 300K legal contracts)?
items.answer: Enterprise RAG budget has three phases — one-time ingestion (~$7.5K for 300K legal contracts, dominated by PDF extraction), monthly storage (~$150–$350 for vector DB + object store), and per-query serving (~$0.008 blended with model tiering) totaling ~$1.5–1.8K/month at 5K queries/day.

items.title: Latency/cost/relevancy tradeoff triangle?
items.prompt: Latency/cost/relevancy tradeoff triangle?
items.answer: Latency, cost, and relevancy form a constrained triangle where cross-encoder reranking is the rare win-win (relevancy ↑, cost ↓, latency ↓ via fewer chunks to LLM), while top-k, model tier, and cache threshold are the primary three-way tradeoff knobs.

items.title: Latency vs throughput for LLM serving?
items.prompt: Latency vs throughput for LLM serving?
items.answer: LLM decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (arithmetic intensity ~2 FLOPs/byte at batch=1, far below the GPU roofline), so larger batches increase GPU utilization and throughput but increase TTFT — tune for latency (small batch, speculative decoding, continuous batching) for interactive workloads and for throughput (large batch, max concurrent sequences, vLLM PagedAttention) for batch pipelines, and reserve ~30% GPU headroom for mixed-workload priority queuing.

items.title: Benchmark each LLM call in multi-step pipeline?
items.prompt: Benchmark each LLM call in multi-step pipeline?
items.answer: Wrap every LLM call in a timing + token-count decorator (prompt_tokens × price_in + completion_tokens × price_out), emit as OTel spans or LangSmith traces to get per-step p95 dashboards, then fix the actual bottleneck — which is usually the reranker or a high-output-token step, not the generation model you assumed.

items.title: Real bottleneck in LLM serving throughput? PagedAttention?
items.prompt: Real bottleneck in LLM serving throughput? PagedAttention?
items.answer: The real LLM serving throughput bottleneck is KV cache memory fragmentation: traditional contiguous-allocation schemes waste 60–80% of GPU HBM (achieving only 20–40% effective utilization), capping batch concurrency far below hardware capacity; PagedAttention borrows OS virtual-memory paging to store KV tensors in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks (>95% HBM utilization, 2–24× throughput gain in the vLLM paper), with prefix caching and KV quantization (FP8) providing further concurrency multipliers.

items.title: When and how implement LLM guardrails?
items.prompt: When and how implement LLM guardrails?
items.answer: Guardrails are a four-layer stack — input classifier (Llama Guard) → system-prompt constraints → synchronous or async output classifier → Presidio PII scrub — with FP rate tuned below 0.5% on real traffic and bypass rate verified via periodic red-team.

items.title: Minimize harmful outputs while staying useful?
items.prompt: Minimize harmful outputs while staying useful?
items.answer: Minimize harm without over-refusal by defining a per-category harm taxonomy, tuning each classifier threshold separately against real traffic (FP < 0.5% for Tier-2, recall > 95% for Tier-1), using a three-zone response model (full / scoped / refused) for borderline queries, and monitoring both harmful output rate and over-refusal rate as independent production KPIs.

items.title: Detect policy violations / offensive content?
items.prompt: Detect policy violations / offensive content?
items.answer: Detect policy violations with a two-boundary, three-tier pipeline: fast regex/blocklist + Llama Guard (Tier-1, synchronous) at input; fine-tuned DistilBERT for company-specific Tier-2 violations (synchronous for high-liability domains, async for medium-risk) at output — with separate precision-recall calibration per harm category and a monthly retraining loop fed by human-reviewed flagged samples.

items.title: Protect against prompt injection and jailbreaking?
items.prompt: Protect against prompt injection and jailbreaking?
items.answer: Prompt injection is an architectural problem (structural defenses: delimiter fencing, injection classifier on input AND retrieved content, tool allowlisting); jailbreaking is an alignment problem (Llama Guard on input + output, system prompt hardening, model upgrade) — layer both because neither alone is sufficient.

items.title: Handle exceptions in GenAI applications?
items.prompt: Handle exceptions in GenAI applications?
items.answer: GenAI exceptions fall into six classes — provider errors (backoff+circuit-breaker), schema violations (Instructor retry-with-error, cap at 2), context overflow (truncation cascade), guardrail blocks (canned response, no retry), hallucinations (faithfulness gate + fallback, not retry), and tool failures (idempotent backoff + loop termination) — each with separate handling and separate observability metrics.

items.title: Constitutional AI and alignment?
items.prompt: Constitutional AI and alignment?
items.answer: Constitutional AI is two phases — supervised finetuning on the model's own critique-and-revise output against sampled written principles, then RLAIF where a model reading those principles produces the *harmlessness* preference labels that a human would have produced in RLHF (helpfulness stays human, PPO/DPO unchanged) — and as an application engineer you ship the pattern, not the training: a routed inference-time critique-and-revise loop costing one extra generation pass, plus one versioned policy document that is simultaneously your system prompt, your LLM-judge rubric, and your human-review…

items.title: Data privacy and PII in prompts and logs?
items.prompt: Data privacy and PII in prompts and logs?
items.answer: PII is a five-boundary problem — ingestion before embedding, query time before the outbound call, the log/trace write path, eval datasets copied from prod, and caches — detected with a hybrid regex+NER pipeline (Presidio, ~98% on structured IDs but only 90–95% on names in prose), de-identified per boundary with redaction for logs and reversible vault tokenization wherever the answer must name a real entity (naive redaction cost ~15 points of retrieval recall), backed by zero-data-retention plus DPAs/BAAs with every processor including the vector DB, subject_id in chunk metadata so erasure is…

items.title: Bias in training data and generated content?
items.prompt: Bias in training data and generated content?
items.answer: Bias enters at four points — pretraining corpus, RLHF annotator pool, *your* retrieval corpus, and *your* prompt/exemplars — and you only control the last two, so the answer is a measurement plan on your own task: counterfactual perturbation testing (swap names, pronouns, dialect; measure score, refusal-rate, tone and *length* deltas with bootstrapped CIs), subgroup performance gaps, and the four-fifths impact ratio (<0.80 flags adverse impact, the LL144 statistic) — mitigate at model/corpus/prompt/scrubbing/schema/threshold layers, run the suite in CI on every prompt diff, and remember a pub…

items.title: Red-team an LLM system?
items.prompt: Red-team an LLM system?
items.answer: Red-teaming is structured evaluation, not improvisation: build a harm taxonomy, cross it with attack classes (direct jailbreak, indirect RAG injection, encoding, multi-turn crescendo, tool abuse, prompt extraction), attack it in three tiers (automated PyRIT/Garak → model-assisted paraphrase → human experts on the catastrophic nodes), measure attack success rate *per node* plus coverage and benign false-positive rate, and wire every confirmed bypass into CI as a permanent regression test.

items.title: Generated code gets executed — prevent malicious code?
items.prompt: Generated code gets executed — prevent malicious code?
items.answer: Contain, don't detect: never eval in-process, isolate in gVisor or a Firecracker microVM, default to zero network egress with the cloud metadata endpoint explicitly blocked, keep all credentials outside the boundary, use one disposable container per request with hard CPU/memory/PID/wall-clock limits, and layer an import allowlist, orchestrator-side tool privilege separation, a human gate for irreversible actions, and full audit logging on top — because generated code is untrusted even when the user is trusted.

items.title: Self-Supervision in LLMs
items.prompt: Explain Self-Supervision in LLMs — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How LLMs learn from unlabeled text via next-token prediction, masked language modeling, and the pretraining objective.

items.title: Seq2Seq Architecture
items.prompt: Explain Seq2Seq Architecture — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Encoder-decoder sequence-to-sequence architecture, attention mechanism, and how it preceded the transformer.

items.title: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
items.prompt: Explain Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: RNN cell, hidden state propagation, vanishing gradient problem, LSTM and GRU variants, and why RNNs gave way to transformers.

items.title: Transformer Architecture Overview
items.prompt: Explain Transformer Architecture Overview — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Full transformer stack: embedding, positional encoding, attention blocks, FFN, residual connections, layer norm, and output projection.

items.title: Prefill & Decode Phases
items.prompt: Explain Prefill & Decode Phases — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The two phases of LLM inference: prefill (parallel prompt processing) vs decode (autoregressive token generation), their compute vs memory bottleneck characteristics, and KV cache role.

items.title: Query, Key, Value Attention
items.prompt: Explain Query, Key, Value Attention — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Self-attention mechanism: Q/K/V projections, scaled dot-product attention, softmax, multi-head attention, and causal masking.

items.title: RWKV Model
items.prompt: Explain RWKV Model — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: RWKV: the RNN-Transformer hybrid that achieves linear complexity inference with transformer-quality results. Receptance, Weight, Key, Value formulation and how it differs from standard attention.

items.title: Chinchilla Scaling Law
items.prompt: Explain Chinchilla Scaling Law — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Hoffmann et al. (2022) optimal compute allocation: equal scaling of model size and tokens. Why Chinchilla showed GPT-3 was undertrained, and how it changed model design.

items.title: LLM Development Bottlenecks
items.prompt: Explain LLM Development Bottlenecks — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The two macro bottlenecks constraining LLM progress: training data (quantity, quality, depletion) and electricity/compute (energy cost, data center capacity, chip availability).

items.title: Post-Training: Why & How
items.prompt: Explain Post-Training: Why & How — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why pretrained models need post-training (factual errors, harmful outputs, instruction-following gaps) and the three main solutions: SFT, preference finetuning (RLHF/DPO), and Best-of-N.

items.title: RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
items.prompt: Explain RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Full RLHF pipeline: SFT → reward model training from human preferences → PPO optimization. Key components, reward hacking, and why it's expensive.

items.title: DPO — Direct Preference Optimization
items.prompt: Explain DPO — Direct Preference Optimization — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How DPO eliminates the reward model and RL loop by directly optimizing on preference pairs. Mathematical intuition, comparison to RLHF, and when to prefer each.

items.title: Best-of-N / Beam Search
items.prompt: Explain Best-of-N / Beam Search — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Inference-time compute scaling via Best-of-N sampling and beam search. How generating multiple candidates and scoring with a reward model improves output quality without retraining.

items.title: Fine-Tuning: When, Why & Decision Framework
items.prompt: Explain Fine-Tuning: When, Why & Decision Framework — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: When to fine-tune vs prompt-engineer vs RAG, the two capabilities it improves (domain knowledge, instruction following), cost realities, and the decision tree for choosing your approach.

items.title: Fine-Tuning Types: Full, Partial, PEFT
items.prompt: Explain Fine-Tuning Types: Full, Partial, PEFT — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Full fine-tuning vs partial (frozen layers) vs Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT). LoRA, adapter-based, and soft prompt methods — tradeoffs in memory, data needs, and serving.

items.title: LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation
items.prompt: Explain LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: LoRA's core idea: freeze original weights, train low-rank decomposition matrices A and B. Rank selection, alpha scaling, how adapters are merged at inference, and QLoRA.

items.title: Model Distillation
items.prompt: Explain Model Distillation — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Knowledge distillation: training a small student model to mimic a large teacher model using soft labels and intermediate representations. The distillation data pipeline path.

items.title: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning & Model Merging
items.prompt: Explain Multi-Task Fine-Tuning & Model Merging — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Simultaneous vs sequential fine-tuning, catastrophic forgetting, and model merging techniques (weight summing, layer stacking, concatenation).

items.title: Fine-Tuning Hyperparameters
items.prompt: Explain Fine-Tuning Hyperparameters — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Learning rate, batch size, epochs, and prompt loss weight — what each controls, typical ranges, and how to tune them systematically.

items.title: Memory Bottlenecks in Fine-Tuning
items.prompt: Explain Memory Bottlenecks in Fine-Tuning — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why fine-tuning needs more memory than inference: forward + backward pass, optimizer states, gradient checkpointing, numerical precision, and quantization.

items.title: Token Sampling: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P
items.prompt: Explain Token Sampling: Temperature, Top-K, Top-P — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How LLMs select the next token: temperature scaling, top-K filtering, nucleus (top-P) sampling — their effects on diversity vs coherence.

items.title: LLM Evaluation Metrics
items.prompt: Explain LLM Evaluation Metrics — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Exact match, lexical similarity (edit distance, ROUGE, BLEU), semantic similarity (cosine), LLM-as-judge, and their biases (self, position, verbosity).

items.title: Evaluation Pipeline Design
items.prompt: Explain Evaluation Pipeline Design — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Turn-based vs task-based evaluation, evaluating the evaluator itself (signal quality, metric-outcome correlation, consistency, cost), and the full evaluation harness.

items.title: Loss Functions: Cross-Entropy & Perplexity
items.prompt: Explain Loss Functions: Cross-Entropy & Perplexity — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Cross-entropy loss for next-token prediction, perplexity as its exponent, KL divergence for distribution comparison — intuition, formulas, and what they measure.

items.title: Model Evaluation Workflow
items.prompt: Explain Model Evaluation Workflow — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Hard vs soft attributes, pointwise vs comparative evaluation, the 5-stage workflow: filter → benchmark → experiment → monitor, and cost-performance frontier mapping.

items.title: Open Weight vs Open Source Models
items.prompt: Explain Open Weight vs Open Source Models — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The distinction between open-weight (weights released, license restrictions) and truly open-source (training data, code, weights all public) — implications for production use.

items.title: Prompt Engineering Strategies
items.prompt: Explain Prompt Engineering Strategies — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Zero/few/one-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, system vs user prompts, persona, output format, self-critique, and iterative refinement strategies.

items.title: Prompt Attacks & Defenses
items.prompt: Explain Prompt Attacks & Defenses — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Prompt injection, jailbreaking, prompt extraction, information extraction — attack vectors and defense strategies with violation rate and false refusal rate metrics.

items.title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.prompt: Explain RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Full RAG pipeline: indexing → querying → retrieval → generation. Term-based vs embedding-based vs hybrid retrieval, chunking, query rewriting, and reranking.

items.title: Vector Search & KNN
items.prompt: Explain Vector Search & KNN — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Embedding-based retrieval, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms (HNSW, IVF, FAISS), exact vs approximate tradeoffs, and two-stage retrieval (cheap retriever + KNN rerank).

items.title: AI Agents: Observe → Decide → Act → Learn
items.prompt: Explain AI Agents: Observe → Decide → Act → Learn — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Agent loop, tool types (knowledge augmentation, capability extension, write actions), planning vs execution separation, observability, and failure modes.

items.title: Agent Memory Systems
items.prompt: Explain Agent Memory Systems — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Short-term (in-context) vs long-term (external storage) memory, why memory matters beyond context window, cross-session persistence, and consistency benefits.

items.title: Dataset Engineering for LLMs
items.prompt: Explain Dataset Engineering for LLMs — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Data formats per task (self-supervised, instruction, preference, reward), quality dimensions, volume estimation, annotation, augmentation, synthesis, and data processing pipeline.

items.title: Inference Optimization
items.prompt: Explain Inference Optimization — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Compute vs memory-bound bottlenecks, quantization, pruning, distillation, speculative decoding, continuous batching, KV cache, prompt caching, and model/tensor parallelism.

items.title: Speculative Decoding
items.prompt: Explain Speculative Decoding — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How a small draft model generates candidate tokens that the large target model verifies in parallel — achieving 2-3x speedup without quality loss.

items.title: Model & Tensor Parallelism
items.prompt: Explain Model & Tensor Parallelism — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Tensor parallelism (split layers across GPUs), pipeline parallelism (split layers sequentially), context parallelism, sequence parallelism — when and why each.

items.title: Agent Observability
items.prompt: Explain Agent Observability — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Tracing, monitoring, and debugging multi-step agent runs — the three pillars of observability (traces, metrics, evaluation), what to instrument, and the tools that matter in production.

items.title: Production LLM Serving
items.prompt: Explain Production LLM Serving — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The decode bottleneck and the three pillars that solve it — PagedAttention, continuous batching, and Flash Attention — converging in vLLM, TGI, and TensorRT-LLM into a unified serving stack.

items.title: Quantization for Inference
items.prompt: Explain Quantization for Inference — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: int8, int4, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF, NF4 — how post-training quantization reduces model size 2-4x with minimal quality loss, and how to choose the right scheme for your deployment.

items.title: KV Cache Management
items.prompt: Explain KV Cache Management — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How the Key-Value cache grows during autoregressive decoding, why it becomes the memory bottleneck at long context, and how PagedAttention, GQA/MQA, and prefix caching manage it.

items.title: Flash Attention
items.prompt: Explain Flash Attention — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How tiled attention keeps computation in SRAM to avoid materializing the full N×N attention matrix in HBM — 2-4x speedup, O(N) memory, mathematically identical output to standard attention.

items.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
items.prompt: Explain Model Context Protocol (MCP) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The open protocol that standardises how LLM applications connect to external tools and data, replacing N×M bespoke integrations with one client/server contract — the host/client/server split, what a server exposes, and why a shared protocol changes agent architecture.

items.title: GRPO & RL with Verifiable Rewards
items.prompt: Explain GRPO & RL with Verifiable Rewards — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Group Relative Policy Optimization drops PPO's critic network and estimates the advantage baseline from the mean reward of a group of sampled completions — the algorithm behind modern reasoning models, paired with verifiable rewards from executable checks rather than a learned preference model.

items.title: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
items.prompt: Explain Mixture of Experts (MoE) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Replacing the dense FFN with many expert FFNs and a router that activates only top-k per token — decoupling total parameters from per-token compute, plus the load-balancing problem that makes or breaks training, shared experts, and why expert parallelism dominates MoE serving cost.

items.title: Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute
items.prompt: Explain Reasoning Models & Test-Time Compute — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Spending more compute at inference instead of training — long chain-of-thought, sampling-and-selection, and effort/budget controls — how the accuracy-vs-inference-compute curve behaves, and where spending more thinking tokens stops paying for itself.

items.title: Structured Output & Constrained Decoding
items.prompt: Explain Structured Output & Constrained Decoding — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How schema enforcement actually works at the token level: compile the schema or grammar to an automaton, and at each step mask the logits of every token that cannot legally continue the parse. Covers JSON mode vs strict schema vs full grammar constraints, the token-boundary problem, and why valid output is not correct output.

items.title: Multimodal Models & VLMs
items.prompt: Explain Multimodal Models & VLMs — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How vision-language models turn pixels into tokens the LLM can attend to — the vision encoder plus projector pattern, native early-fusion alternatives, image tiling and resolution handling, and why image tokens dominate the context budget in document-heavy workloads.

items.title: Long-Context Techniques
items.prompt: Explain Long-Context Techniques — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How context windows grew from thousands to millions of tokens: RoPE and its scaling variants (position interpolation, NTK-aware, YaRN), ALiBi, and sparse or compressed attention — plus why a bigger window does not fix mid-context recall, prefill latency, or KV-cache memory.

items.title: Prompt Caching Mechanics
items.prompt: Explain Prompt Caching Mechanics — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Caching the prefill KV state of a stable prompt prefix so repeat requests skip recomputation — exact-prefix matching semantics, why any byte change invalidates everything after it, cache-write vs cache-read pricing, TTLs, and how to order a prompt so the cache actually hits.

items.title: Model Routing & Cost Cascades
items.prompt: Explain Model Routing & Cost Cascades — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Sending each request to the cheapest model that can handle it — routers that classify difficulty up front versus cascades that escalate on a confidence or verification signal, how to calibrate the threshold on a golden set, and why the narrowing price gap between tiers changed the economics.

items.title: Agent Evaluation Methodology
items.prompt: Explain Agent Evaluation Methodology — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Evaluating multi-step agents where the final answer hides the process — outcome versus trajectory evaluation, programmatic checks against LLM-as-judge and its known biases, per-step attribution of failures, and building a regression suite that survives non-determinism.

items.title: Caching Strategies
items.prompt: Explain Caching Strategies — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Cache placement, read/write patterns (cache-aside, write-through, write-behind, write-around), invalidation approaches, and the three named failure modes: thundering herd, penetration, avalanche.

items.title: Queues and Backpressure
items.prompt: Explain Queues and Backpressure — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Work queues vs event logs, delivery guarantees (at-least-once plus idempotency), per-key ordering, and backpressure mechanisms that keep overload from silently turning into unbounded latency.

items.title: Consistency Trade-offs
items.prompt: Explain Consistency Trade-offs — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: CAP restated correctly via PACELC, the consistency spectrum (strong/sequential/causal/eventual), session guarantees, database isolation levels, and quorum math (W+R>N).

items.title: Sharding and Partitioning
items.prompt: Explain Sharding and Partitioning — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Range vs hash vs consistent-hash partitioning, shard-key selection criteria, the noisy-neighbour problem, fixed-partition-count rebalancing, and local vs global secondary indexes.

items.title: Idempotency
items.prompt: Explain Idempotency — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why at-least-once delivery makes idempotency non-negotiable, the idempotency-key pattern (client-generated, atomic check-and-store), natural idempotency via conditional writes, and HTTP method semantics.

items.title: Circuit Breakers and Bulkheads
items.prompt: Explain Circuit Breakers and Bulkheads — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Circuit breaker states (closed/open/half-open) and required fallback behavior, bulkheads as resource partitioning to limit blast radius, and the supporting cast: timeouts, jittered backoff, retry budgets.

items.title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
items.prompt: Explain Change Data Capture (CDC) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why dual writes aren't atomic, log-based CDC off the replication log (WAL/binlog/oplog) vs trigger-based vs query-based, and the transactional outbox pattern for explicit event-schema control.

items.title: Rate Limiting
items.prompt: Explain Rate Limiting — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Protection vs compliance limiting, algorithm comparison (token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed/sliding window), distributed rate limiting across a fleet, and cost-based limiting for variable-cost requests.

items.title: Load Balancing
items.prompt: Explain Load Balancing — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: L4 vs L7 load balancing, algorithm choice (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, weighted), health checks, and connection draining during deploys.

items.title: Service Discovery
items.prompt: Explain Service Discovery — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Client-side vs server-side service discovery, DNS-based discovery, and service registries (Consul, etcd, ZooKeeper) — how services find each other as instances scale up and down.

items.title: Consensus Algorithms (Raft/Paxos)
items.prompt: Explain Consensus Algorithms (Raft/Paxos) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Leader election and distributed consensus — how a cluster agrees on a single value despite node failures, why majority quorums prevent split-brain, and why consensus is expensive and reserved for metadata rather than data-plane traffic.

items.title: Database Replication
items.prompt: Explain Database Replication — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Leader-follower vs multi-leader vs leaderless replication, synchronous vs asynchronous replication, replication lag, and failover mechanics when a follower falls behind or a leader dies.

items.title: Distributed Transactions (2PC & Saga)
items.prompt: Explain Distributed Transactions (2PC & Saga) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Two-phase commit and its coordinator-blocking failure mode, the Saga pattern (choreography vs orchestration) with compensating actions, TCC, and why atomic multi-service transactions are avoided in practice.

items.title: Concurrency Control (Optimistic, Pessimistic, MVCC)
items.prompt: Explain Concurrency Control (Optimistic, Pessimistic, MVCC) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking, and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) — how databases let readers and writers avoid blocking each other, and when optimistic locking's retry cost bites.

items.title: Distributed Locking and Fencing Tokens
items.prompt: Explain Distributed Locking and Fencing Tokens — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Distributed locks (Redlock, lease-based locks) and why a naive lock built on a single key is dangerous under GC pauses or clock drift, and how fencing tokens close the gap between lock expiry and actual work completion.

items.title: Event Sourcing and CQRS
items.prompt: Explain Event Sourcing and CQRS — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Storing state as an append-only sequence of events and separating write models from read models (CQRS) — rebuilding current state by replay, and the operational cost of eventual consistency between the two sides.

items.title: Observability (Metrics, Logs, Traces)
items.prompt: Explain Observability (Metrics, Logs, Traces) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The three pillars — metrics, logs, and distributed traces — plus SLIs/SLOs/SLAs and error budgets, and how they compose to answer 'is the system healthy' and 'why did this one request fail.'

items.title: API Design and Evolution
items.prompt: Explain API Design and Evolution — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL tradeoffs, backward-compatible schema evolution, and pagination strategies (offset vs cursor-based) — designing APIs that can change without breaking existing clients.

items.title: Indexing and Storage Engines (B-tree vs LSM-tree)
items.prompt: Explain Indexing and Storage Engines (B-tree vs LSM-tree) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: B-tree vs LSM-tree storage engines — why B-trees favor read-heavy in-place-update workloads and LSM-trees favor write-heavy workloads via compaction, and how this drives database engine choice.

items.title: Zero-Downtime Deployments
items.prompt: Explain Zero-Downtime Deployments — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Blue-green, canary, and rolling deployment strategies, plus the expand-contract pattern for safe schema migrations — shipping changes without a maintenance window or a broken in-flight request.

items.title: Multi-Region Architecture
items.prompt: Explain Multi-Region Architecture — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Active-active vs active-passive multi-region designs, cross-region latency, data residency constraints, and conflict resolution (last-write-wins, CRDTs) when the same data is writable in two regions.

items.title: Connection Pooling and Resource Exhaustion
items.prompt: Explain Connection Pooling and Resource Exhaustion — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Connection pool sizing, exhaustion, and the counterintuitive failure mode where increasing pool size makes an overloaded database worse — pool-per-dependency as a bulkhead, and external pooling (PgBouncer-style).

items.title: Logical Clocks and Causality (Lamport & Vector Clocks)
items.prompt: Explain Logical Clocks and Causality (Lamport & Vector Clocks) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why wall-clock timestamps can't order distributed events (clock skew, NTP step/slew), Lamport timestamps and the happens-before relation, vector clocks as the mechanism that actually detects concurrency (per-node counters, increment-on-send, element-wise max on receive), version vectors and Dynamo-style sibling detection, and why last-write-wins silently loses concurrent writes.

items.title: Ranking Ties Three Ways
items.prompt: Ranking Ties Three Ways (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, ties) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill how ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK diverge on a leaderboard containing tied scores, showing that only RANK leaves gaps in the sequence and only ROW_NUMBER is non-deterministic unless the ORDER BY breaks ties on a unique column.

items.title: Day-over-Day Revenue Change with LAG
items.prompt: Day-over-Day Revenue Change with LAG (LAG, window functions, NULL handling, PARTITION BY) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill computing the absolute and percentage change from the previous day with LAG, including what the first row of every partition returns and why a NULL default silently swallows the first period.

items.title: Time to Next Order with LEAD
items.prompt: Time to Next Order with LEAD (LEAD, window functions, per-customer partitioning, date arithmetic) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill using LEAD partitioned by customer to measure the gap in days until each customer's next order, and handling the trailing row where no next order exists.

items.title: Running Total and the RANGE-versus-ROWS Peer Trap
items.prompt: Running Total and the RANGE-versus-ROWS Peer Trap (running totals, window frames, ROWS vs RANGE, duplicate ORDER BY keys) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a cumulative revenue total with SUM OVER, exposing that the default RANGE frame lumps all rows sharing an ORDER BY value into one peer group so same-day rows all show the day-end total instead of a row-by-row cumulative.

items.title: Seven-Day Moving Average of Signups
items.prompt: Seven-Day Moving Average of Signups (moving averages, window frames, ROWS BETWEEN, partial windows) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a trailing seven-row moving average with an explicit ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING frame, and decide what the first six rows should report when the window is not yet full.

items.title: Share of Category Total and Quartile Buckets
items.prompt: Share of Category Total and Quartile Buckets (window aggregates, PARTITION BY, NTILE, percent of total) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill emitting a per-row percentage of its category total using an aggregate window function that does not collapse rows, then bucketing the same rows into quartiles with NTILE in a single pass.

items.title: Employees and Their Managers
items.prompt: Employees and Their Managers (self-joins, LEFT JOIN, hierarchical data, NULL parents) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a self-join of an employee table onto itself on manager_id so every employee shows their manager's name, and why an INNER JOIN silently drops the top-level employee whose manager_id is NULL.

items.title: Customers Who Never Ordered
items.prompt: Customers Who Never Ordered (anti-joins, NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN IS NULL, EXCEPT) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill the three equivalent spellings of an anti-join -- LEFT JOIN with an IS NULL filter, NOT EXISTS, and EXCEPT -- and why the IS NULL predicate must sit in the WHERE clause rather than the ON clause.

items.title: The NOT IN NULL Trap
items.prompt: The NOT IN NULL Trap (NOT EXISTS vs NOT IN, three-valued logic, NULL semantics, anti-joins) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill why NOT IN against a subquery whose column contains even one NULL returns zero rows under three-valued logic, and how NOT EXISTS gives the intended answer unchanged.

items.title: Join Fan-Out Double Counting
items.prompt: Join Fan-Out Double Counting (join fan-out bugs, double counting, pre-aggregation, one-to-many joins) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill an order total that is silently inflated because the order row is joined to both line items and payments at once, and fix it by pre-aggregating each child table to one row per order before joining.

items.title: Overlapping Bookings on the Same Room
items.prompt: Overlapping Bookings on the Same Room (self-joins, interval overlap, inequality join predicates, deduplicating pairs) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill an inequality self-join that finds every pair of bookings on the same room whose date intervals overlap, using the start-before-other-end and end-after-other-start condition and an id comparison to avoid reporting each pair twice.

items.title: Latest Order per Customer with LATERAL
items.prompt: Latest Order per Customer with LATERAL (LATERAL join, correlated subqueries, top-1 per group, join alternatives) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a correlated LATERAL join that fetches each customer's most recent order row, and contrast it with the window-function and correlated-subquery formulations on both readability and access pattern.

items.title: Categories Above a Sales Threshold
items.prompt: Categories Above a Sales Threshold (GROUP BY + HAVING, WHERE vs HAVING, aggregate filters) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill filtering groups on an aggregate with HAVING while a row-level predicate stays in WHERE, and show how moving one predicate between the two clauses changes the result.

items.title: Counting Rows, Values and Distinct Values
items.prompt: Counting Rows, Values and Distinct Values (COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col), COUNT DISTINCT, NULL handling, aggregate semantics) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill the difference between COUNT(*), COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column) on a table with NULLs and repeats, and why AVG over a nullable column divides by the non-NULL count rather than the row count.

items.title: Pivoting Monthly Revenue into Columns
items.prompt: Pivoting Monthly Revenue into Columns (pivoting, conditional aggregation, CASE WHEN inside aggregates, FILTER clause) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill turning one row per month into one column per month with SUM(CASE WHEN ...) conditional aggregation, plus the FILTER (WHERE ...) spelling, and note why a pivot with an unknown column set needs generated SQL.

items.title: Median Without a Builtin
items.prompt: Median Without a Builtin (median/percentiles without a builtin, ROW_NUMBER, even vs odd counts, self-join on rank) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill computing an exact median from row counts and ordinal positions when no MEDIAN function exists, correctly averaging the two middle values on an even row count and per group rather than overall.

items.title: Ninety-Fifth Percentile Latency by Endpoint
items.prompt: Ninety-Fifth Percentile Latency by Endpoint (median/percentiles without a builtin, percentile interpolation, NTILE, nearest-rank vs linear) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill computing a p95 latency per endpoint without PERCENTILE_CONT, choosing explicitly between the nearest-rank definition and linear interpolation between neighbouring order statistics and showing they disagree on small samples.

items.title: Subtotals and Grand Totals in One Result Set
items.prompt: Subtotals and Grand Totals in One Result Set (GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, subtotal rows, GROUPING() flag) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill producing region, region-plus-product and grand-total rows from one scan with ROLLUP or GROUPING SETS, and using GROUPING() to tell a real NULL apart from a subtotal placeholder.

items.title: Refactoring Nested Subqueries into CTEs
items.prompt: Refactoring Nested Subqueries into CTEs (CTEs, non-recursive CTEs, query readability, multi-step aggregation) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill rewriting a triple-nested inline-view query as a chain of named non-recursive CTEs that each do one step, keeping the result identical while making the aggregation order explicit.

items.title: Generating a Complete Date Spine
items.prompt: Generating a Complete Date Spine (recursive CTEs, date spine, missing dates, LEFT JOIN to a calendar) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill building a contiguous calendar of dates with a recursive CTE and left-joining sparse event data onto it so days with zero events appear as zero rather than vanishing from the report.

items.title: Walking the Org Chart
items.prompt: Walking the Org Chart (recursive CTEs, hierarchies, depth level, materialized path) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a recursive CTE that walks a manager hierarchy from a given root, carrying a depth counter and an accumulated path string, and distinguishing UNION from UNION ALL in the recursive term.

items.title: Consecutive Login Streaks
items.prompt: Consecutive Login Streaks (gaps-and-islands, recursive CTEs, ROW_NUMBER offset trick, streak length) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill the gaps-and-islands date-minus-row-number trick to collapse consecutive daily logins into islands and report each user's longest streak, including the deduplication needed when a user logs in twice a day.

items.title: Collapsing Overlapping Date Ranges
items.prompt: Collapsing Overlapping Date Ranges (gaps-and-islands, interval merging, running maximum, window functions) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill merging overlapping and adjacent subscription intervals per customer into minimal disjoint ranges by starting a new island whenever a row's start exceeds the running maximum end date of all prior rows.

items.title: Cycle-Safe Reachability in a Graph
items.prompt: Cycle-Safe Reachability in a Graph (recursive CTEs, graph traversal, cycle detection, visited path guard) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill a recursive CTE over a directed edge table that finds every node reachable from a start node while carrying a visited-path string to break cycles that would otherwise make the recursion never terminate.

items.title: Bucketing Events into Days, Weeks and Months
items.prompt: Bucketing Events into Days, Weeks and Months (date bucketing, strftime, week start alignment, truncation vs formatting) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill truncating timestamps into day, ISO-week and month buckets with date functions, and why grouping on a formatted string sorts correctly only when the format is zero-padded and year-first.

items.title: Monthly Cohort Retention Matrix
items.prompt: Monthly Cohort Retention Matrix (cohort/retention, cohort month, month offset, retention denominator) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill assembling a retention matrix that groups users by their first-purchase month and counts, for each subsequent month offset, how many of that cohort were active, with the cohort size as the denominator throughout.

items.title: Funnel Conversion Rates by Step
items.prompt: Funnel Conversion Rates by Step (funnel conversion, step counts, conditional aggregation, step-to-step rates) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill counting distinct users reaching each funnel step and reporting both overall and step-to-step conversion rates, ensuring counts are monotonically non-increasing because a later step implies the earlier one.

items.title: Funnel Steps That Must Happen In Order
items.prompt: Funnel Steps That Must Happen In Order (funnel conversion, event ordering, timestamp constraints, self-joins) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill an order-preserving funnel where each step only counts if its timestamp is strictly after the previous step's, and show how the naive per-step EXISTS version overcounts users who did the steps out of sequence.

items.title: Sessionizing Clickstream with a 30-Minute Timeout
items.prompt: Sessionizing Clickstream with a 30-Minute Timeout (sessionization, inactivity timeout, LAG, cumulative sum session id) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill splitting a per-user event stream into sessions by flagging every event whose gap from the previous event exceeds a thirty-minute inactivity threshold and turning a running sum of those flags into a session identifier.

items.title: Week-over-Week Growth on a Gap-Free Calendar
items.prompt: Week-over-Week Growth on a Gap-Free Calendar (date bucketing, LAG, growth rate, zero-filled periods) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill week-over-week growth where weeks with no activity must appear as zero, so the comparison uses a gap-free week series rather than LAG over only the weeks that happen to have rows.

items.title: Top Three Products per Category
items.prompt: Top Three Products per Category (top-N per group, ROW_NUMBER, RANK for ties, correlated subquery alternative) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill top-N per group with a partitioned ROW_NUMBER filtered in an outer query, and decide when RANK is the right choice instead because tied Nth-place rows must all be kept.

items.title: Deleting Exact Duplicate Rows
items.prompt: Deleting Exact Duplicate Rows (deduplication, exact duplicates, ROW_NUMBER keep-one, rowid) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill removing exact duplicate rows from a table with no primary key by numbering rows within each duplicate group and keeping only the first, and why a plain SELECT DISTINCT does not solve the deletion.

items.title: Collapsing Near-Duplicate Customer Records
items.prompt: Collapsing Near-Duplicate Customer Records (deduplication, near-duplicates, normalized match key, survivorship rules) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill collapsing near-duplicate contacts that differ only by casing, whitespace and punctuation by grouping on a normalized match key, then picking a surviving record with an explicit tie-break on completeness and recency.

items.title: Building a Type-2 Slowly Changing Dimension
items.prompt: Building a Type-2 Slowly Changing Dimension (slowly changing dimensions, SCD2, valid_from/valid_to, is_current flag) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.
items.answer: Drill turning a stream of dimension snapshots into SCD type 2 rows with valid_from, valid_to and is_current, closing each version with the next change's timestamp and emitting a new version only when a tracked attribute actually changed.

items.title: Latest Row per Key with QUALIFY
items.prompt: Latest Row per Key with QUALIFY (top-N per group, QUALIFY, window filtering, dialect differences) — write the query/derivation from scratch and say what makes the naive version wrong.

items.prompt: Group Anagrams [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.

items.prompt: Top K Frequent Elements [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer: Count freqs in a map; bucket each value by its count in an array of size n+1; scan buckets high→low until k values collected.

items.title: Product of Array Except Self
items.prompt: Product of Array Except Self [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer: Fill answer with left-running products in one pass, then multiply each cell by right-running products in a second pass — no division, O(1) extra space.

items.title: Valid Sudoku
items.prompt: Valid Sudoku [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer: One pass over the board: for each digit, if it's already in that row's, column's, or box's set, return false; otherwise add it to all three sets.

items.title: Encode and Decode Strings
items.prompt: Encode and Decode Strings [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer: Encode each string as len + "#" + payload; decode by reading digits until #, then slice exactly len characters — payload content never affects parsing.

items.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
items.prompt: Longest Consecutive Sequence [Medium] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer: Hash all nums into a set; for each num where num-1 is missing, walk forward counting num, num+1, ... in the set and track the max length.

items.title: Valid Palindrome
items.prompt: Valid Palindrome [Easy] — state the pattern, the invariant, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.

items.answer: Sort, fix i, two-pointer the rest for -nums[i]; on hit record triplet and skip dupes at i, left, and right.

Synthesize new minority-class rows by interpolating between a minority point and one of its k minority-class nearest neighbours at a random position along the segment. Getting it right means excluding a point from its own neighbour list and handling a minority class with fewer than k+1 members, where the naive neighbour search returns fewer candidates than requested.

items.title: Implement Linear Regression with Gradient Descent
items.prompt: Implement Linear Regression with Gradient Descent — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: fit_linear_gd(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, lr: float, n_iters: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float, list[float]] # weights, bias, loss_history

Fit weights and a bias by repeatedly stepping down the MSE gradient, recording the loss each iteration. The parts that actually break: omitting the 2/n normalization so a working learning rate silently depends on dataset size, and not tracking loss to notice divergence when the step is too large for unscaled features.

items.title: Implement Linear Regression via the Normal Equation
items.prompt: Implement Linear Regression via the Normal Equation — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: fit_linear_normal(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float] # weights, bias

Solve for the closed-form OLS coefficients on a design matrix with an intercept column appended. The non-trivial bit is not forming an explicit inverse of X^T X at all — use a solve or lstsq — because the Gram matrix is singular the moment two features are collinear or n is smaller than d.

items.title: Implement Ridge Regression in Closed Form
items.prompt: Implement Ridge Regression in Closed Form — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: fit_ridge(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, lam: float) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float] # weights, bias

Add an L2 penalty to the closed-form solution, solving (X^T X + lam * I) w = X^T y. The detail interviewers watch for is that the intercept must not be penalized — the penalty matrix carries a zero in the bias position — and that lam is only comparable across features when they are standardized first.

items.title: Implement Logistic Regression with Cross-Entropy Loss
items.prompt: Implement Logistic Regression with Cross-Entropy Loss — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: fit_logistic(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, lr: float, n_iters: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, float, list[float]] # weights, bias, loss_history

Gradient descent on the binary cross-entropy of a sigmoid over a linear score. Two things sink naive implementations: exp overflowing for large-magnitude logits, and log(0) producing NaN once a prediction saturates — both fixed by a branch-stable sigmoid and computing the loss from logits rather than from clipped probabilities.

items.title: Implement Multinomial Logistic Regression
items.prompt: Implement Multinomial Logistic Regression — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: fit_softmax_regression(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, n_classes: int, lr: float, n_iters: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # W of shape (d, n_classes), b of shape (n_classes,)

Extend logistic regression to K classes with a softmax over class scores and one-hot targets. The gradient is deceptively simple — X^T (P - Y) — but only if the softmax subtracts a per-row max before exponentiating and the weight matrix keeps a consistent (d, K) orientation through both the forward pass and the update.

items.title: Implement Multinomial Naive Bayes with Laplace Smoothing
items.prompt: Implement Multinomial Naive Bayes with Laplace Smoothing — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class MultinomialNB(alpha: float) with fit(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> None, predict_log_proba(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray and predict(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

Estimate class priors and per-feature conditional likelihoods from a document-term count matrix, then classify by the argmax of summed log probabilities. Smoothing is the whole exercise: without the +alpha in the numerator and alpha * vocab_size in the denominator, one word never seen with a class zeroes that class's entire posterior.

items.title: Implement k-Nearest Neighbours with a KD-Tree
items.prompt: Implement k-Nearest Neighbours with a KD-Tree — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: build_kdtree(X: np.ndarray) -> KDNode and knn_query(tree: KDNode, q: np.ndarray, k: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # neighbour indices, distances (both sorted ascending)

Build a KD-tree by recursively splitting on the median of a cycling axis, then answer queries with a search that keeps a bounded max-heap of the k best candidates. The correctness hinge is the prune test: the far subtree must still be descended whenever the distance to the splitting plane is smaller than the current k-th best distance, or the query silently returns wrong neighbours.

items.title: Implement Best-Split Search with Gini and Entropy
items.prompt: Implement Best-Split Search with Gini and Entropy — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: best_split(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, criterion: str) -> tuple[int, float, float] # feature_index, threshold, gain

Scan every feature and every candidate threshold to find the split that maximizes information gain under either impurity measure. What separates a working answer from a quadratic one is sorting each feature once and updating the left/right class counts incrementally as the threshold sweeps, instead of recomputing impurity over both halves at every candidate.

items.title: Implement a CART Decision Tree
items.prompt: Implement a CART Decision Tree — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class DecisionTree(max_depth: int, min_samples_split: int, criterion: str) with fit(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> None and predict(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

Recursively apply the best split to grow a binary tree with stopping rules on depth, minimum samples and zero gain, plus a predict that routes each row down to a leaf. The bugs live in the base cases: a node where every candidate split leaves one child empty must become a leaf rather than recursing forever on the same rows.

items.title: Implement Gradient Boosting with Decision Stumps
items.prompt: Implement Gradient Boosting with Decision Stumps — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class GradientBoostingStumps(n_stages: int, lr: float) with fit(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> None and predict_proba(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

Fit an additive ensemble of depth-1 trees, each trained on the negative gradient of log-loss with respect to the current additive score. The step that trips people up is shrinkage: each stump's leaf values must be scaled by the learning rate before being added to the running score, and the ensemble starts from the log-odds of the base rate rather than from zero.

items.title: Implement K-Means with K-Means++ Initialization
items.prompt: Implement K-Means with K-Means++ Initialization — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: kmeans(X: np.ndarray, k: int, seed: int, max_iter: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, float] # centroids, labels, inertia

Lloyd's assign-and-update iteration run to convergence on top of D^2-weighted seeding. Two cases must be handled explicitly: a centroid that loses all its points, which has to be reseeded at the farthest point instead of producing a NaN mean, and the k-means++ sampling weights when duplicate points make a squared distance exactly zero.

items.title: Implement PCA via SVD and via Eigendecomposition
items.prompt: Implement PCA via SVD and via Eigendecomposition — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: pca_svd(X: np.ndarray, n_components: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray] and pca_eig(X: np.ndarray, n_components: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # components (k, d), explained_variance (k,), mean (d,)

Center the data and recover the same principal axes two ways: as eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and as right singular vectors of the centered matrix. The gotcha is sign ambiguity — the two routes return components that may differ by a factor of -1, so any comparison has to be up to sign — and that the SVD route is the numerically stable one because forming X^T X squares the condition number.

items.title: Implement Precision Recall and F1 Score
items.prompt: Implement Precision Recall and F1 Score — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: precision_recall_f1(y_true: np.ndarray, y_pred: np.ndarray, average: str) -> tuple[float, float, float]

Derive the four confusion counts from label arrays and compute the three metrics, with macro and micro averaging over multiple classes. The case that must not crash is a class the model never predicts: precision is 0/0 there, and the answer has to be a documented convention (zero) rather than a NaN that silently poisons the macro average.

items.title: Implement ROC-AUC from Scratch
items.prompt: Implement ROC-AUC from Scratch — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: roc_auc(y_true: np.ndarray, y_score: np.ndarray) -> float

Sweep every distinct score threshold to trace the TPR/FPR curve and integrate it with the trapezoid rule, or equivalently compute the rank-based Mann-Whitney statistic. Tied scores are the trap: they must collapse into a single threshold point and receive averaged ranks, otherwise the curve gains spurious staircase steps and the area comes out wrong.

items.title: Implement Numerically Stable Softmax and Cross-Entropy
items.prompt: Implement Numerically Stable Softmax and Cross-Entropy — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: softmax(logits: np.ndarray, axis: int) -> np.ndarray and cross_entropy_from_logits(logits: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, np.ndarray] # mean loss, dlogits

A softmax with the max-subtraction shift and a cross-entropy that consumes logits directly, together with the combined backward pass. The whole exercise is the log-sum-exp shift that stops exp overflowing at a logit of 1000, and the log(0) that appears the moment you compose a separately computed softmax with a naive log.

items.title: Implement a Two-Layer Neural Net with Manual Backprop
items.prompt: Implement a Two-Layer Neural Net with Manual Backprop — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class TwoLayerNet(d_in: int, d_hidden: int, n_classes: int, seed: int) with forward(X: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray, loss_and_grads(X: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, dict[str, np.ndarray]] and step(grads: dict, lr: float) -> None

Forward through affine, ReLU, affine and softmax cross-entropy, then hand-derive every gradient back to the first layer's weights and bias. Two errors account for most wrong answers: the transpose in dW = A.T @ dZ, and applying the ReLU backward mask to the post-activation instead of the pre-activation.

items.title: Implement Numerical Gradient Checking
items.prompt: Implement Numerical Gradient Checking — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: grad_check(f: Callable[[np.ndarray], float], grad_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], theta: np.ndarray, eps: float) -> float # max relative error over all entries

A generic checker that perturbs each parameter by plus and minus eps and compares the central difference against the analytic gradient using relative error. The details that make it usable: central differences (error O(eps^2), not the O(eps) of a forward difference), a relative-error denominator guarded against zero, and knowing that ReLU kinks produce legitimate false failures.

items.title: Implement Inverted Dropout Forward and Backward
items.prompt: Implement Inverted Dropout Forward and Backward — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: dropout_forward(X: np.ndarray, p: float, training: bool, seed: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] and dropout_backward(dout: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray # out, mask, then dX

Sample a Bernoulli mask at train time, scale surviving activations by 1/(1-p) so the expectation matches eval time, and pass through unchanged when not training. The interviewer is checking that the identical mask is reused in the backward pass and that the inverted scaling lives in training rather than as a rescale at inference.

items.title: Implement Batch Normalization Forward and Backward
items.prompt: Implement Batch Normalization Forward and Backward — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: batchnorm_forward(x: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, beta: np.ndarray, running_mean: np.ndarray, running_var: np.ndarray, momentum: float, eps: float, training: bool) -> tuple[np.ndarray, tuple] and batchnorm_backward(dout: np.ndarray, cache: tuple) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # dx,…

Normalize each feature over the batch, apply the learnable gain and shift, maintain running statistics for eval mode, then derive the backward pass. The backward is the hard part: the batch mean and variance both depend on every input in the batch, so dx has three coupled terms and cannot be written as a simple elementwise product with dout.

items.title: Implement the Adam Optimizer
items.prompt: Implement the Adam Optimizer — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class Adam(shape: tuple, lr: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, eps: float) with step(params: np.ndarray, grads: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray # returns updated params

Exponential moving averages of the gradient and its square, bias-corrected, with epsilon in the denominator outside the square root. Bias correction is the piece people skip and it matters most in the first dozen steps, where an uncorrected first moment is biased toward zero and the effective step comes out far too small.

items.title: Implement Scaled Dot-Product Attention
items.prompt: Implement Scaled Dot-Product Attention — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: scaled_dot_product_attention(Q: np.ndarray, K: np.ndarray, V: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray | None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # output, attn_weights

Compute QK^T scaled by 1/sqrt(d_k), apply a causal or padding mask, softmax, and take the weighted sum of V. Two things must be right: masking by adding a large negative value before the softmax rather than zeroing weights afterwards, and the 1/sqrt(d_k) scale, without which a large d_k drives the softmax into near one-hot saturation with vanishing gradients.

items.title: Implement Multi-Head Attention
items.prompt: Implement Multi-Head Attention — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class MultiHeadAttention(d_model: int, n_heads: int, seed: int) with forward(x: np.ndarray, mask: np.ndarray | None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # output (batch, seq, d_model), per-head attn weights

Project Q, K and V, reshape into heads, attend per head, then concatenate and apply the output projection. The whole difficulty is reshape-and-transpose bookkeeping between (batch, seq, n_heads * d_head) and (batch, n_heads, seq, d_head) — a transpose applied in the wrong order silently mixes the head and time axes and still produces output of the correct shape.

items.title: Implement Layer Normalization
items.prompt: Implement Layer Normalization — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: layernorm_forward(x: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, beta: np.ndarray, eps: float) -> tuple[np.ndarray, tuple] and layernorm_backward(dout: np.ndarray, cache: tuple) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # dx, dgamma, dbeta

Normalize over the feature axis of each token independently, apply the learnable gain and bias, and derive the backward pass. What separates it from batch norm is that statistics are per example, so behaviour is identical in training and eval and there are no running statistics to maintain — but dx still has the three-term structure because the mean and variance depend on every feature in the row.

items.title: Implement Sinusoidal Positional Encodings
items.prompt: Implement Sinusoidal Positional Encodings — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: sinusoidal_positional_encoding(max_len: int, d_model: int) -> np.ndarray # shape (max_len, d_model)

Build the (max_len, d_model) table of sines and cosines over geometrically spaced frequencies. The implementation detail that matters is computing the frequency term in log space as exp(-log(10000) * 2i / d_model) rather than as a direct power that underflows for large d_model, and putting sin on even dimensions with cos on odd.

items.title: Implement a TF-IDF Vectorizer
items.prompt: Implement a TF-IDF Vectorizer — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: class TfidfVectorizer with fit(corpus: list[str]) -> None, transform(corpus: list[str]) -> np.ndarray and a vocabulary_ dict[str, int] attribute

Build a vocabulary from a corpus, compute term frequencies and smoothed inverse document frequencies, and L2-normalize each document row. The variants are what make it fiddly: which smoothing (the +1s in log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1) and whether normalization runs before or after IDF weighting decide whether your numbers match anyone else's.

items.title: Implement Cosine Similarity and Top-K Retrieval
items.prompt: Implement Cosine Similarity and Top-K Retrieval — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: cosine_topk(queries: np.ndarray, corpus: np.ndarray, k: int) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray] # top_k_indices (n_queries, k), scores (n_queries, k)

Normalize the embedding matrix once so cosine similarity collapses to a single matrix product, then return the k highest-scoring corpus rows per query. The efficiency point is np.argpartition rather than a full argsort of every row, and the correctness point is guarding a zero-norm vector from turning the whole score row into NaN.

items.title: Implement Beam Search Decoding
items.prompt: Implement Beam Search Decoding — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: beam_search(step_fn: Callable[[list[int]], np.ndarray], beam_width: int, max_len: int, eos_id: int, alpha: float) -> list[tuple[list[int], float]] # hypotheses ranked by length-normalized score

Expand the top-b partial hypotheses at each step against a next-token log-probability function, carrying cumulative log-probs. Two things must be handled: a finished hypothesis is set aside rather than re-expanded, or it keeps accumulating negative log-prob and loses unfairly, and length normalization, without which beam search systematically prefers short outputs.

items.title: Implement BPE Tokenizer Training
items.prompt: Implement BPE Tokenizer Training — state the signature, the invariant that must hold, and the time/space complexity before writing any code.
items.answer:
Contract: train_bpe(corpus: list[str], n_merges: int) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, str]], dict[str, int]] and encode_bpe(word: str, merges: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> list[str] # merge list, vocab; then symbols

Count adjacent symbol pairs across a word-frequency table, merge the most frequent pair, and repeat for n merges, producing an ordered merge list plus the resulting vocabulary. The subtleties: pair counts must be weighted by word frequency rather than by word type, ties need a deterministic tiebreak, and encoding new text has to replay merges in learned order instead of greedily matching the longest symbol.

items.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
items.prompt: Explain Bias-Variance Tradeoff — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How model complexity trades off bias (underfitting) against variance (overfitting), and why total error is minimized at an intermediate complexity.

items.title: Bayes' Theorem
items.prompt: Explain Bayes' Theorem — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Prior, likelihood, and posterior — how Bayes' theorem updates beliefs given evidence, and its role in Naive Bayes, A/B testing, and calibration.

items.title: Central Limit Theorem
items.prompt: Explain Central Limit Theorem — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why sample means of any distribution approach a normal distribution as sample size grows, and why this underlies confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

items.title: Hypothesis Testing & A/B Significance
items.prompt: Explain Hypothesis Testing & A/B Significance — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Null vs alternative hypotheses, p-values, Type I/II errors, and statistical power — the machinery behind A/B test significance calls.

items.title: MLE vs MAP Estimation
items.prompt: Explain MLE vs MAP Estimation — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Maximum likelihood estimation vs maximum a posteriori estimation, and how a prior regularizes MLE — the probabilistic view of L2 regularization.

items.title: Linear Regression
items.prompt: Explain Linear Regression — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Ordinary least squares, the normal equation, and gradient descent fitting a line — assumptions (linearity, homoscedasticity) and when they break.

items.title: Logistic Regression
items.prompt: Explain Logistic Regression — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Sigmoid link function, log-odds, decision boundary, and maximum likelihood estimation for binary classification.

items.title: SVM & Maximum Margin
items.prompt: Explain SVM & Maximum Margin — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
