items.title: Decision Trees
items.prompt: Explain Decision Trees — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Recursive binary splitting, impurity measures (Gini, entropy), and how greedy splits build a tree — plus why deep trees overfit.

items.title: k-Nearest Neighbors
items.prompt: Explain k-Nearest Neighbors — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Instance-based classification by majority vote among the k nearest neighbors, the curse of dimensionality, and the bias-variance effect of k.

items.title: Naive Bayes Classifier
items.prompt: Explain Naive Bayes Classifier — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Conditional independence assumption, how it simplifies Bayes' theorem for classification, and why it works well for text despite the naive assumption.

items.title: Bagging vs Boosting
items.prompt: Explain Bagging vs Boosting — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Bootstrap aggregating (variance reduction via parallel models) vs boosting (bias reduction via sequential residual fitting) — the two ensemble philosophies.

items.title: Random Forest
items.prompt: Explain Random Forest — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Bagging plus random feature subsampling — how decorrelating trees reduces variance further than bagging alone, and feature importance from impurity decrease.

items.title: Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM)
items.prompt: Explain Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: How XGBoost/LightGBM fit trees to the negative gradient of the loss, shrinkage (learning rate), and why boosting dominates tabular data leaderboards.

items.title: Stacking Ensembles
items.prompt: Explain Stacking Ensembles — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Combining heterogeneous base models via a meta-learner trained on out-of-fold predictions — when stacking beats simple averaging.

items.title: k-Means Clustering
items.prompt: Explain k-Means Clustering — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Centroid initialization, the assign-update Lloyd's algorithm loop, and the elbow method for choosing k.

items.title: Hierarchical Clustering
items.prompt: Explain Hierarchical Clustering — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Agglomerative clustering with linkage criteria (single, complete, average, Ward) and reading a dendrogram to choose cluster count.

items.title: DBSCAN Density Clustering
items.prompt: Explain DBSCAN Density Clustering — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Density-based clustering via core points, border points, and noise — eps/min_samples parameters and why DBSCAN finds arbitrary-shaped clusters k-means can't.

items.title: Principal Component Analysis
items.prompt: Explain Principal Component Analysis — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: PCA as variance-maximizing projection — eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, explained variance ratio, and dimensionality reduction tradeoffs.

items.title: t-SNE & UMAP
items.prompt: Explain t-SNE & UMAP — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Nonlinear dimensionality reduction for visualization — how t-SNE/UMAP preserve local neighborhood structure and why global distances aren't meaningful.

items.title: Cross-Validation Strategies
items.prompt: Explain Cross-Validation Strategies — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: K-fold, stratified, and time-series splits — how cross-validation estimates generalization error and avoids the single-split variance trap.

items.title: Confusion Matrix & Metrics
items.prompt: Explain Confusion Matrix & Metrics — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Precision, recall, F1, and specificity derived from the confusion matrix — how threshold choice trades off false positives against false negatives.

items.prompt: Explain ROC vs Precision-Recall Curves — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: ROC-AUC vs precision-recall AUC — why PR curves are more informative than ROC on imbalanced classes, and how to read both.

items.title: Learning Curves Diagnosis
items.prompt: Explain Learning Curves Diagnosis — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Training vs validation error as a function of training set size — diagnosing high bias (both plateau high) vs high variance (large gap) from the curve shape.

items.title: Gradient Descent Variants
items.prompt: Explain Gradient Descent Variants — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.

items.title: L1 vs L2 Regularization
items.prompt: Explain L1 vs L2 Regularization — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: L1 (Lasso) vs L2 (Ridge) penalties — why L1's diamond constraint region produces sparse weights while L2's circular region shrinks smoothly.

items.title: Dropout & Batch Normalization
items.prompt: Explain Dropout & Batch Normalization — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Dropout as approximate model averaging via random unit masking, and batch normalization's effect on internal covariate shift and training stability.

items.title: Backpropagation
items.prompt: Explain Backpropagation — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.

items.title: CNNs & Convolution
items.prompt: Explain CNNs & Convolution — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Convolutional filters sliding over input, stride, padding, and pooling — how CNNs build translation-invariant hierarchical feature detectors.

items.prompt: Explain RNN, LSTM & GRU — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.

items.prompt: Explain Weight Init & Vanishing Gradients — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why naive weight initialization causes vanishing/exploding activations and gradients, and how Xavier/He initialization keeps variance stable across layers.

items.title: Feature Scaling
items.prompt: Explain Feature Scaling — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Normalization vs standardization vs robust scaling — which algorithms require scaling (gradient descent, kNN, SVM) and which don't (trees), and why.

items.title: Categorical Encoding
items.prompt: Explain Categorical Encoding — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: One-hot, ordinal, target, and embedding encodings for categorical features — the cardinality/leakage tradeoffs of each.

items.title: Handling Imbalanced Data
items.prompt: Explain Handling Imbalanced Data — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Class imbalance techniques — random oversampling, SMOTE, class weighting, and threshold tuning — and how each reshapes the decision boundary.

items.title: Recommender Systems
items.prompt: Explain Recommender Systems — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Collaborative filtering (user-based, item-based, matrix factorization) vs content-based filtering, and hybrid architectures used in production recommenders.

items.title: A/B Testing for ML Products
items.prompt: Explain A/B Testing for ML Products — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Randomized experiment design for ML products — sample size/power calculation, novelty effects, and common pitfalls like peeking and Simpson's paradox.

items.title: Time Series Decomposition
items.prompt: Explain Time Series Decomposition — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Decomposing a time series into trend, seasonality, and residual components (additive vs multiplicative), and why decomposition guides model choice.

items.title: ARIMA Forecasting
items.prompt: Explain ARIMA Forecasting — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: AR, I, MA components of ARIMA, stationarity and differencing, and reading ACF/PACF plots to choose model order.

items.title: Gaussian Mixture Models & EM
items.prompt: Explain Gaussian Mixture Models & EM — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Mixtures of Gaussians fit by expectation-maximization — soft responsibilities instead of k-means' hard assignments, the E-step posterior and M-step closed-form updates, covariance types (full, tied, diagonal, spherical), and choosing the number of components by BIC/AIC.

items.title: Probability Calibration
items.prompt: Explain Probability Calibration — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Making predicted scores behave like real probabilities — Platt (sigmoid) scaling vs isotonic regression and their data requirements, reliability curves, Brier score and its refinement/calibration decomposition, expected calibration error, and why resampling or class weighting for imbalance destroys calibration and forces a recalibration step.

items.title: Feature Importance & Interpretability
items.prompt: Explain Feature Importance & Interpretability — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Explaining what a model learned — permutation importance, partial dependence plots with their feature-independence assumption plus per-instance ICE curves, SHAP values aggregated from local to global (and TreeSHAP), LIME and its instability across reruns, and the impurity/Gini importance bias toward high-cardinality features together with the fix.

items.title: Causal Inference Basics
items.prompt: Explain Causal Inference Basics — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Getting causal effects from observational data — confounding and why correlation is not causation, potential outcomes and counterfactuals, propensity score matching and inverse propensity weighting, difference-in-differences and its parallel-trends assumption, instrumental variables (relevance plus the exclusion restriction), regression discontinuity, and uplift modeling for who to treat.

items.title: Nested CV & Model Comparison Tests
items.prompt: Explain Nested CV & Model Comparison Tests — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why reusing one cross-validation loop for both hyperparameter tuning and reporting gives an optimistically biased score, the nested inner-tuning/outer-evaluation structure and its k_inner x k_outer cost, and the statistical tests for declaring one model better — Dietterich's 5x2cv paired t-test, McNemar's test, DeLong's test for correlated AUCs, and multiple-comparison correction.

items.title: Design a Feed Ranking System
items.prompt: Design a Feed Ranking System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
The home feed of a social product: every pull returns a ranked page of posts drawn from follows, groups, and recommended sources. Candidate generation must cut 500M items to ~500 in under 20ms while the ranker's per-item feature fetch — not the model forward pass — is what actually consumes the 150ms p99 budget.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 300M
  • feed requests per user per day: 20
  • items in corpus: 500M
  • candidates after retrieval: 500
  • features per candidate: 200
  • bytes per feature: 8
  • p99 latency budget ms: 150
  • retention days: 90

items.title: Design a Model Serving Platform
items.prompt: Design a Model Serving Platform — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A shared inference platform that hosts hundreds of teams' models behind one gRPC endpoint with per-model autoscaling, versioning, and shadow traffic. The tension is that batching is the only way to reach acceptable GPU utilization, yet every millisecond spent waiting to fill a batch is subtracted from a 50ms p99 budget that also has to cover queueing and network hops.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 150M
  • inference calls per user per day: 40
  • models hosted: 400
  • avg model size gb: 4
  • gpu memory gb: 80
  • per replica throughput qps: 600
  • batch window ms: 10
  • p99 latency budget ms: 50

items.title: Design a Feature Store
items.prompt: Design a Feature Store — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A central store that serves precomputed entity features online at request time and materializes the same definitions offline for training. The hard part is numeric: one ranking request fans out to hundreds of online key lookups, while the offline side must hold years of point-in-time-correct history whose row count and bytes-per-row decide whether backfills cost thousands or millions.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 200M
  • requests per user per day: 25
  • online feature reads per request: 300
  • entities in online store: 1B
  • features per entity: 800
  • bytes per feature: 8
  • daily feature writes: 50B
  • offline retention days: 730

items.title: Design a Search Ranking System
items.prompt: Design a Search Ranking System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
Web-scale or in-app search where a typed query must return relevance-ordered results from a twenty-billion-document index. Retrieval breadth and ranking quality pull against each other inside one budget: widening the L1 candidate set improves recall but multiplies the L2 reranker's per-query cost, and the index's shard count sets a fan-out floor on tail latency.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 500M
  • searches per user per day: 10
  • documents in index: 20B
  • avg indexed terms per doc: 600
  • bytes per posting entry: 8
  • l1 candidates per query: 10000
  • l2 reranked docs per query: 200
  • p99 latency budget ms: 200

items.title: Design an Embedding Retrieval System
items.prompt: Design an Embedding Retrieval System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A vector retrieval service that answers approximate nearest-neighbour queries over a billion item embeddings for recommendation and semantic search callers. Recall, memory, and latency are one joint constraint: raw float32 vectors will not fit in RAM at this corpus size, so quantization and graph parameters must be chosen against an explicit index-bytes and shard-count budget rather than by feel.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 250M
  • retrieval calls per user per day: 30
  • items in corpus: 1B
  • embedding dim: 768
  • bytes per dim float32: 4
  • hnsw graph degree: 32
  • recall at 100 target: 0.95
  • p99 latency budget ms: 30

items.title: Design an Ads CTR Prediction System
items.prompt: Design an Ads CTR Prediction System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
The auction path of an ad server, where predicted click-through rate multiplied by bid decides which of thousands of eligible ads wins each impression. Predictions must be calibrated in absolute probability rather than merely well-ordered, because revenue is priced off the number — and the training pipeline that produces that number ingests tens of billions of heavily imbalanced impression rows per day under an 80ms serving budget.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 400M
  • ad requests per user per day: 50
  • candidate ads per request: 2000
  • scored ads per request: 500
  • positive click rate: 0.02
  • bytes per impression row: 400
  • training window days: 30
  • p99 latency budget ms: 80

items.title: Design a Real-Time Personalization System
items.prompt: Design a Real-Time Personalization System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A system that folds a user's last few minutes of behaviour — taps, dwells, skips, searches — into the very next ranking call, so a session visibly adapts as it happens. Freshness is the whole product, so the design has to hold a live per-session state in memory for every concurrent user and update it within seconds of each event, while the event stream itself arrives at an order of magnitude higher rate than the serving traffic.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 180M
  • events per user per day: 120
  • personalization requests per user per day: 25
  • peak concurrent sessions: 12M
  • session state bytes: 2048
  • event bytes: 300
  • freshness target seconds: 5
  • p99 latency budget ms: 100

items.title: Design a Fraud Detection Pipeline
items.prompt: Design a Fraud Detection Pipeline — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
An inline risk decision on every payment authorization: approve, challenge, or decline before the transaction completes. The load-bearing features are velocity counters over 1-minute to 30-day windows that must be read and updated synchronously inside a 250ms budget, while a fraud base rate near 0.1% and a chargeback label lag of weeks decide how much data a retrain actually has to learn from.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 80M
  • transactions per user per day: 7.5
  • peak to average ratio: 4
  • velocity windows: 1m/5m/1h/24h/30d
  • bytes per transaction row: 1200
  • fraud base rate: 0.001
  • label lag days: 45
  • decision latency budget ms: 250
  • retention days: 400

items.title: Design a Push Notification Ranking System
items.prompt: Design a Push Notification Ranking System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A daily pipeline that scores every candidate notification for every user and sends only the few worth interrupting them for, subject to per-user frequency caps and quiet hours. The interesting constraint is a batch one: tens of billions of user-candidate pairs must be scored inside a fixed nightly window, and the send-versus-suppress threshold is an economic decision about long-run engagement rather than a per-item probability.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 250M
  • registered devices: 600M
  • candidates per user per day: 40
  • target sends per user per day: 3
  • scoring window hours: 4
  • bytes per scored row: 120
  • p99 delivery latency budget ms: 500
  • retention days: 180

items.title: Design an ETA Prediction System
items.prompt: Design an ETA Prediction System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
The arrival-time estimate shown in a ride-hailing or delivery app, recomputed continuously as a trip progresses and as traffic changes underneath it. Millions of GPS pings per second must be aggregated into fresh per-road-segment speed features and joined to a route of hundreds of segments inside a 120ms budget, so the geospatial feature fan-out — not the model — is what dominates both latency and storage.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 40M
  • trips per user per day: 1.2
  • eta queries per trip: 8
  • road segments: 60M
  • segments per route: 300
  • telemetry pings per second: 2M
  • bytes per ping: 80
  • p99 latency budget ms: 120
  • retention days: 365

items.title: Design a Content Moderation Pipeline
items.prompt: Design a Content Moderation Pipeline — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A pipeline that screens hundreds of millions of daily uploads — text, images, video — for policy violations, blocking the clearest cases inline and routing the uncertain ones to human reviewers. The economics are a cascade problem: an expensive multimodal model cannot run on every upload, so cheap high-recall filters must set thresholds that keep the human review queue inside the reviewer headcount the business can actually staff.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 700M
  • uploads per user per day: 0.7
  • avg media bytes mb: 1.8
  • tier1 auto clear rate: 0.98
  • human review rate: 0.005
  • reviewer items per hour: 120
  • p99 inline latency budget ms: 300
  • retention days: 180

items.title: Design an Experimentation Platform
items.prompt: Design an Experimentation Platform — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
The A/B infrastructure every model launch has to pass through: deterministic variant assignment, exposure logging, and a metrics pipeline that reports lift with confidence intervals. Assignment must be a sub-millisecond local computation at full request QPS while exposure logs — one row per user per experiment per session — become the largest table in the company, and sample-size math decides whether an experiment can even detect the effect it was designed for.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 300M
  • assignment calls per user per day: 60
  • concurrent experiments: 1200
  • exposure event bytes: 180
  • metrics tracked: 800
  • baseline conversion rate: 0.04
  • min detectable effect: 0.005
  • retention days: 180

items.title: Design a Near-Duplicate Detection System
items.prompt: Design a Near-Duplicate Detection System — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A service that decides, at upload time, whether a new item is a near-copy of something already in an eight-billion-item corpus — for reposts, plagiarism, or spam clustering. Exact pairwise comparison is quadratic and impossible at this size, so the whole design rests on signature-based bucketing whose band and permutation counts trade recall against index bytes and candidate-set size in a way you must actually compute.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 600M
  • uploads per user per day: 0.7
  • corpus items: 8B
  • minhash permutations: 128
  • lsh bands: 16
  • bytes per signature: 512
  • similarity threshold: 0.8
  • p99 latency budget ms: 40
  • retention days: 1095

items.title: Design an LLM Inference Serving Platform
items.prompt: Design an LLM Inference Serving Platform — whiteboard it end to end: candidate generation, features, ranking, serving budget, and how it is evaluated online.
items.answer:
A hosted platform serving a 70B-parameter model to chat and API clients with streamed tokens, continuous batching, and tenant-level quotas. Capacity here is set by KV-cache memory rather than compute: model weights plus per-token cache determine how many concurrent sequences fit on a GPU, and that concurrency number is what fixes time-to-first-token, tokens per second per user, and cost per thousand requests.

Scale to quote:
  • dau: 20M
  • requests per user per day: 15
  • avg prompt tokens: 1200
  • avg output tokens: 400
  • model params billions: 70
  • bytes per param: 2
  • kv cache bytes per token: 320KB
  • gpu memory gb: 80
  • p99 ttft budget ms: 800
  • target output tokens per second per user: 30

items.title: Data Validation for ML Pipelines
items.prompt: Explain Data Validation for ML Pipelines — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Schema and distribution assertions run on every batch before it reaches training — TFDV schema inference and Great Expectations suites catching null-rate spikes, unseen categorical values, and silently rescaled units before they become a quietly worse model.

items.title: Dataset Versioning
items.prompt: Explain Dataset Versioning — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Content-addressed dataset snapshots (DVC-style pointers, table-format time travel) so a training run can be replayed against the exact rows it saw, and why treating the query as the version breaks the moment a late-arriving row lands.

items.title: Reproducible Feature Engineering Pipelines
items.prompt: Explain Reproducible Feature Engineering Pipelines — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: One transformation definition shared by the batch and online paths, with fitted statistics (means, encoders, bucket edges) persisted as artifacts instead of recomputed — the fix for the classic bug where the serving path re-fits a scaler on live traffic.

items.title: Feature Stores
items.prompt: Explain Feature Stores — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: An offline store for training and an online store for low-latency lookup behind a single feature definition — materialization jobs, TTLs, and entity keys — plus the honest question of when a feature store is over-engineering versus a plain cache plus a shared library.

items.title: Online and Offline Feature Parity
items.prompt: Explain Online and Offline Feature Parity — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Detecting the divergence between the feature values a model trained on and the ones it sees at inference by logging served features back to the offline store and running a scheduled parity job on the overlap — the failure that never raises an exception.

items.title: Point-in-Time Correct Feature Joins
items.prompt: Explain Point-in-Time Correct Feature Joins — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Joining labels to the feature values as of the label's event time rather than the latest value — the as-of join and its watermark and TTL edge cases that keep future information from leaking into training and inflating offline AUC.

items.title: Training-Serving Skew
items.prompt: Explain Training-Serving Skew — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The three sources of skew — divergent transformation code, divergent data (training on a filtered sample), and feedback-loop skew from the model's own predictions — and how each shows up as offline metrics that do not survive contact with production.

items.title: Experiment Tracking
items.prompt: Explain Experiment Tracking — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Logging params, metrics, artifacts, and the git SHA per run so a result can be found and rebuilt months later — MLflow and W&B run hierarchies, nested sweeps, and why an untracked notebook run is not a result.

items.title: ML Pipeline Orchestration
items.prompt: Explain ML Pipeline Orchestration — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: DAG-based orchestration of ingest, validate, train, evaluate, and register steps in Airflow, Dagster, or Kubeflow — retries, idempotent task boundaries, backfills, and the sensors that stop a stalled upstream from silently training on stale data.

items.title: Model Registry and Stage Promotion
items.prompt: Explain Model Registry and Stage Promotion — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Immutable model versions with stage transitions (staging, production, archived), the metadata that must ride along (training dataset hash, metrics, input signature), and why serving resolves a registry alias rather than a filesystem path.

items.title: Offline Evaluation Gates
items.prompt: Explain Offline Evaluation Gates — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Automated promotion gates comparing a candidate against the incumbent on holdout and on named slices, with minimum-improvement and no-regression thresholds — and why a single aggregate metric happily promotes a model that is broken for one segment.

items.title: Batch, Online, and Streaming Inference
items.prompt: Explain Batch, Online, and Streaming Inference — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Precomputed batch scoring, request-time online inference, and streaming scoring off an event log — chosen by feature freshness requirements, prediction cardinality, and latency budget rather than by preference, and the point where batch precompute stops being possible.

items.title: Serving Latency Budgets
items.prompt: Explain Serving Latency Budgets — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Decomposing an end-to-end p99 budget across feature lookup, model forward pass, and network hops — why the p99 of the whole is not the sum of the p99s, and how a fan-out to N parallel feature lookups lets the tail dominate.

items.title: Shadow Deployment
items.prompt: Explain Shadow Deployment — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Mirroring live traffic to a candidate model whose predictions are logged but never served — what it catches (latency regressions, feature-pipeline breakage, prediction-distribution shift) and the whole class of effects it cannot measure because nothing acts on the prediction.

items.title: Canary Rollout for Models
items.prompt: Explain Canary Rollout for Models — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Ramping a new model version through traffic percentages with automated analysis at each step — guardrail metrics, minimum sample size per stage, and the auto-rollback rule that has to fire before a bad model reaches full traffic.

items.title: Champion-Challenger Promotion
items.prompt: Explain Champion-Challenger Promotion — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Running a challenger continuously against the production champion on the same traffic and promoting only on a sustained win — how it differs from a one-shot canary, and the selection bias from judging a challenger on traffic the champion itself shaped.

items.title: A/B Testing Models in Production
items.prompt: Explain A/B Testing Models in Production — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Randomizing users rather than requests into model variants, sizing the test for power on the business metric, and the traps that flip a verdict: peeking, interference between users, and novelty effects that decay by week two.

items.title: Production Model Monitoring and Alerting
items.prompt: Explain Production Model Monitoring and Alerting — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The four layers worth instrumenting — system health, input data quality, prediction distribution, and model quality once labels land — plus alert thresholds tuned so that drift pages a human only when it is actionable.

items.title: Data Drift vs Concept Drift
items.prompt: Explain Data Drift vs Concept Drift — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Input distribution shift in P(X) versus a changed relationship P(y|X) — why data drift is often harmless while concept drift always costs accuracy, and why only the first is detectable before labels arrive.

items.title: Population Stability Index
items.prompt: Explain Population Stability Index — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: PSI as the binned symmetric divergence between a reference and a current distribution, the 0.1 and 0.25 rules of thumb, and the binning and sample-size choices that make it fire on noise or miss a real shift entirely.

items.title: KS Test vs KL Divergence
items.prompt: Explain KS Test vs KL Divergence — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Two different questions asked of the same two samples: the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic as the maximum CDF gap with a p-value that shrinks with sample size, versus KL divergence as an unbounded asymmetric information measure that needs smoothing when a bin goes empty.

items.title: Online Drift Detection with ADWIN
items.prompt: Explain Online Drift Detection with ADWIN — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Sequential detectors that flag change without a fixed reference window — ADWIN shrinking its adaptive window when two sub-windows differ, and DDM or Page-Hinkley on an error stream — for when a nightly batch PSI job reacts far too slowly.

items.title: Label Lag and Delayed Ground Truth
items.prompt: Explain Label Lag and Delayed Ground Truth — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: When labels arrive days later or never — fraud chargebacks, churn, loan default — true model quality is unmeasurable exactly when it matters, so proxy metrics, label maturity curves, and the censoring bias of scoring only the labels that have landed carry the load.

items.title: Retraining Triggers and Cadence
items.prompt: Explain Retraining Triggers and Cadence — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Scheduled versus triggered retraining — drift thresholds, performance-degradation triggers, and data-volume triggers — plus the cost of retraining too eagerly: prediction churn, unstable explanations, and a feedback loop that trains on the previous model's own output.

items.title: Model Governance and Lineage
items.prompt: Explain Model Governance and Lineage — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: The provenance chain a regulated deployment must be able to answer for — which data, code, and hyperparameters produced this prediction — plus approval workflows, model cards, and retaining the artifacts needed to reproduce a decision months after it was made.

items.title: Slice-Based Fairness Monitoring
items.prompt: Explain Slice-Based Fairness Monitoring — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Tracking metrics per protected and business-critical segment instead of in aggregate — disparity ratios, the minimum slice support needed for a stable estimate, and the Simpson's-paradox case where the aggregate improves while every slice degrades.

items.title: CI/CD for ML
items.prompt: Explain CI/CD for ML — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Pipelines that test code, data, and model together — unit tests on transformations, schema contract tests, a training smoke run, and an evaluation gate — where the promoted artifact is an immutable model version rather than a freshly rebuilt image.

items.title: GPU Serving and Autoscaling
items.prompt: Explain GPU Serving and Autoscaling — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Dynamic batching and concurrency limits to keep a GPU fed, why request-rate autoscaling misfires on GPU-bound inference when queue depth and batch occupancy are the real signals, and the cold-start cost of loading model weights onto a fresh node.

items.title: Incident Response for ML Systems
items.prompt: Explain Incident Response for ML Systems — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Why an ML incident often has no error rate to page on, the runbook ordering that rolls back to the last known-good version before diagnosing, and the distinct root causes to separate: upstream schema change, feature-pipeline failure, drift, and a bad promotion.

items.title: Cost Management for ML Infrastructure
items.prompt: Explain Cost Management for ML Infrastructure — mechanism, why it matters, and one production tradeoff.
items.answer: Where ML spend actually goes — idle GPUs, repeated feature backfills, and always-on endpoints for low-traffic models — and the levers against it: spot instances with checkpointing, multi-model endpoints, quantization, and scale-to-zero for bursty traffic.

  • What is your strategy when the context window fills up — truncate, summarize, or paginate?

items.title: Section 6 — Auth, Security & Multitenancy
items.prompt: Section 6 — Auth, Security & Multitenancy — whiteboard this section end to end.
items.answer:
